questions.q: What does Level 2 market data show that Level 1 does not?
options: The full depth of the order book -- every price level with resting orders and aggregate quantity, not just the best bid/ask/last trade
The identity of every individual trader placing orders
Level 2 and Level 1 show exactly the same information
Only historical trades from previous trading days
questions.explain: Level 1 gives only the touch (best bid/ask/last trade); Level 2 reveals the full depth behind it, letting a trader assess how thin or deep the book actually is.

questions.q: Under the maker-taker fee model, what happens when an order ADDS liquidity (rests on the book and gets filled)?
options: It typically earns a rebate -- the exchange pays the order
It typically costs a fee identical to removing liquidity
Adding liquidity is always free with no rebate or fee either way
Adding liquidity is charged double the taker fee
questions.explain: Exchanges want deep resting liquidity, so they typically subsidize it with a rebate -- the opposite of the fee charged for removing liquidity.

questions.q: Why do exchanges deliberately reward adding liquidity and charge for removing it?
options: Deep, resting liquidity makes the exchange's market more attractive to trade on, so they subsidize the behavior that creates it and charge the behavior that consumes it
This fee structure is purely arbitrary with no underlying business reason
Removing liquidity is technically more difficult for the exchange to process
Adding liquidity actually costs the exchange more money to support
questions.explain: This is a deliberate piece of market design -- rewarding the behavior (resting orders) that makes a venue more liquid and attractive, which is a competitive advantage for the exchange itself.

questions.q: What does a tiered fee schedule mean for a firm's trading economics?
options: The exact same strategy, run at higher monthly volume, earns a meaningfully better rebate/fee rate per share -- scale itself becomes a real structural advantage
All firms receive identical rebate and fee rates regardless of volume
Higher-volume firms are charged worse rates as a penalty for size
Fee tiers only apply to options trading, never equities
questions.explain: Fee tiers reward higher monthly volume with better rates -- meaning the same quoting logic can be meaningfully more profitable for a large firm than a small one, purely from scale.

questions.q: Why would a market-making strategy's profitability differ between a firm trading 2 million shares/month and one trading 60 million, using identical quoting logic?
options: The 60-million-share firm likely qualifies for a better fee tier, earning a higher rebate per share on the exact same trading activity
Trading volume has no effect on fee rates in any real exchange
Only the firm's quoting logic determines profitability, never its volume
Larger firms are always charged higher fees as a penalty
questions.explain: Tiered fee schedules mean the larger firm earns a meaningfully better rebate rate on identical trading logic -- a real, quantifiable scale advantage separate from strategy quality.
